title: Ward Site (15McL11), McLean County
summary: In McLean County, the Ward Site is a Late Archaic shell-midden cemetery where WPA crews catalogued 433 human burials in 1938.
bodyMarkdown:
The Ward site, recorded as 15McL11, is an Archaic shell-midden site in McLean County. It belongs to a remarkable group of sites left by the [Green River Archaic](https://heritage.ky.gov/Documents/Green-River-Archaic.pdf) people, hunters and gatherers who lived in the region roughly 6,000 to 3,000 years ago.

## Shell middens

Archaeologists have recorded more than 1,700 prehistoric sites in Butler, Ohio, Henderson, McLean and Muhlenberg counties. About 50 of them are considered truly exceptional. Many contain enormous heaps of freshwater mussel shell, built up over centuries of daily life. Because the shell made the soil less acidic, bone and other remains survived unusually well. Mussels mattered, but fish, deer and nuts were also readily available.

## The 1938 excavation

During the Depression, Works Progress Administration crews dug at seven shell midden sites in the region under University of Kentucky professor William S. Webb. Together these digs recovered tens of thousands of artifacts and more than 3,000 burials of humans and dogs. A photo of a McLean County dig shows excavation went on year-round, with an oil-drum heater in the trench.

At Ward, [more than 16,000 square feet](https://www.revistas.unam.mx/index.php/eab/article/view/30866) were carefully excavated in 1938. That area represents about 16 percent of the site.

## Who lived at Ward?

A later skeletal study by Richard Meindl, Robert Mensforth and Heather York used the Ward burials to reconstruct the age structure of the community. The authors argue that the cemetery fully represents a once-living population. They compared Ward with [Indian Knoll](/stories/indian-knoll-ohio-county/) and [Carlston Annis](/stories/carlston-annis-shell-mound/), whose burials show young age distributions and short life expectancies.

Scholars read the way of life differently. One account describes the Green River Archaic people as mobile, moving with the seasons rather than living in one spot all year. Another, based on the Ward evidence, argues for year-round occupation and treats the community as sedentary fisher-hunter-gatherers.

## Kentucky today

[Indian Knoll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Knoll) became a National Historic Landmark in 1964, and other Kentucky shell midden sites have since received the same designation. Many of these places remain on private land, protected by landowners who take their role as stewards seriously. The careful records kept by the 1930s crews are what made the later Ward age study possible.
